query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase FCC CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy, controlled thermal aging induces subtle grain-boundary segregation (e.g., of Mn or Cr) that reduces local cohesive strength, leading to premature crack initiation and brittle behavior under low-temperature or impact loading conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenous, single-phase FCC CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy produced by rapid quenching to ensure uniform distribution of elements.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal aging treatment by annealing the alloy near 400°C for 150–250 hours under an inert atmosphere, carefully calibrated to promote atomic-scale grain-boundary segregation without causing bulk intermetallic or coarse precipitate formation.
generation.conditions: Test and compare two sets of samples: one set subjected to the thermal aging treatment and one as-quenched control. Mechanical testing (tensile and low-temperature impact tests) will be performed under service-relevant conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Subtle atomic-scale segregation of elements (such as Mn or Cr) at the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The localized segregation at grain boundaries decreases the cohesive energy of these interfaces, reducing their ability to blunt advancing cracks under service loads and low-temperature conditions. This degradation in boundary integrity provokes early crack initiation, distinct from the conventional mechanisms driven by coarse precipitate formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Aged samples are expected to exhibit reduced toughness, evidenced by lower fracture energy, reduced elongation at fracture, and earlier crack initiation compared to the as-quenched samples. High-resolution characterizations (e.g., atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM) should reveal measurable atomic enrichment at the grain boundaries in the aged samples.
generation.baseline: The as-quenched, single-phase CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy, with uniformly distributed grain boundary compositions and high ductility/toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is predicted to operate under conditions where the alloy is exposed to prolonged moderate thermal exposure (around 400°C) and subsequently subjected to low-temperature or high-strain-rate loading. At significantly higher temperatures or under different mechanical regimes, other deformation or failure mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact extent of toughness degradation and the critical threshold for beneficial versus detrimental segregation remain to be determined. Fine-tuning of the aging parameters is required to balance segregation without triggering secondary phase precipitation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples: one group undergoes the controlled thermal aging treatment (at 400°C for an optimized duration between 150–250 hours) and another is retained in the as-quenched state. Mechanical testing (tensile tests and Charpy impact tests at low temperatures) alongside microstructural analysis (atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM) are performed.
measurements: Fracture energy and elongation at fracture from mechanical tests
Crack initiation and propagation behavior from fracture surface imaging
Grain-boundary elemental distribution from atom probe or TEM analyses
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in toughness (i.e., similar fracture energy and ductility as the as-quenched controls) and no measurable grain-boundary segregation is detected, then the hypothesis that subtle GB segregation is responsible for brittleness will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

During the tensile test process at intermediate temperatures in the air, intermetallic phases were not yet formed in coarse-grained Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEAs, owing to a short testing time (a few minutes). In addition, the above-mentioned oxide and hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms can be ruled out because these alloys show good resistance to oxidation at intermediate temperatures and hydrogen embrittlement at relatively low hydrogen concentrations (, ). These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.

proposals.material_system: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy in a single-phase FCC state
proposals.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal aging treatment to promote subtle grain-boundary segregation without triggering bulk second-phase precipitation
proposals.conditions: Anneal near 400°C for 150–250 hours versus a rapidly quenched baseline at room temperature, and then test under low-temperature impact and tensile conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale segregation of specific elements (e.g., slight enrichment in Mn or Cr) along grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Even in the absence of large-scale intermetallic precipitates, minor compositional inhomogeneities at the boundaries reduce cohesive strength, leading to premature crack nucleation under service loads at low temperatures
proposals.predicted_outcome: Aged samples exhibit a measurable drop in toughness (lower fracture energy and premature crack propagation) relative to the baseline, with atom probe tomography confirming grain-boundary segregation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This study directly tests whether grain-boundary segregation – a mechanism well-known in conventional alloys – still governs toughness degradation in HEAs, despite their overall phase stability, and defines service boundaries (e.g., low-temperature embrittlement) relevant to engineering applications.

proposals.material_system: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with an initial random FCC structure
proposals.intervention: Induce controlled plastic deformation (high strain rate pre-straining) followed by a moderate anneal to trigger stress-assisted short-range ordering at grain boundaries
proposals.conditions: Pre-strain samples at high strain rates (e.g., in drop-weight impact tests) and then anneal at 300–350°C for short durations (e.g., 1–2 hours) compared with an undeformed control
proposals.structural_mediator: Development of localized short-range order (SRO) along grain boundaries that alters the atomic configuration
proposals.mechanism: The combination of mechanical stress and annealing promotes local compositional reordering at boundaries, which diminishes their ability to blunt cracks, initiating brittle failure mechanisms that are distinct from conventional precipitate-driven embrittlement
proposals.predicted_outcome: Pre-strained-and-annealed samples will show lower toughness (earlier crack initiation in fracture tests) compared to as-quenched, unstrained samples, with electron diffraction and high-resolution TEM evidencing the formation of SRO at GBs
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By comparing mechanically pre-strained and annealed samples with unstrained baselines, this direction distinguishes a new mechanism (stress-induced SRO at GBs) from conventional precipitation, revealing a novel pathway for toughness degradation in HEAs under dynamic service loading.

proposals.material_system: AlxCrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy (compositionally complex and single-phase)
proposals.intervention: Introduce a trace amount of a refractory element (e.g., a few atomic % of tungsten) during alloy synthesis
proposals.conditions: Process using standard arc melting followed by homogenization annealing at high temperature (around 1100°C for 24 hours) then controlled cooling, with mechanical testing at elevated temperatures simulating service conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Localized chemical heterogeneity at grain boundaries due to the tendency of tungsten to slow diffusion and promote slight boundary clustering
proposals.mechanism: The refractory dopant, while maintaining the overall single-phase nature, segregates subtly under service conditions and creates local stiffness mismatches that act as crack precursors under high-temperature loading
proposals.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-doped HEA will show a marked reduction in toughness (in terms of lower fracture strain and impact energy) in high-temperature tests compared to the undoped baseline, with microstructural characterization (via TEM and EDS mapping) confirming tungsten enrichment at grain boundaries
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This comparison probes whether alloying-induced local chemical heterogeneity, unique to compositionally complex HEAs, can trigger a transition to brittle behavior even without conventional intermetallic formation, thereby extending our understanding of toughness degradation mechanisms.

proposals.material_system: FeCoNiCrMn high-entropy alloy in its FCC single-phase form
proposals.intervention: Introduce low levels of interstitial elements (carbon or nitrogen) by controlled carburization/nitriding
proposals.conditions: Expose the HEA to a carburizing or nitriding atmosphere at 600°C for short durations (e.g., 2–4 hours) ensuring retention of the FCC phase, then perform bending and tensile tests at room and sub-ambient temperatures
proposals.structural_mediator: Interstitial atom segregation at the grain boundaries, possibly forming a thin, chemically distinct layer
proposals.mechanism: Interstitial atoms preferentially migrate to and cluster at grain boundaries, reducing the cohesive strength and ductility of boundaries under stress, thus initiating brittle fracture even in the absence of coarse precipitates
proposals.predicted_outcome: The interstitial-doped samples will show decreased ductility and toughness (with a lower elongation at fracture and impact resistance) compared to pristine samples, with surface and boundary analyses (using SIMS and high-resolution TEM) confirming interstitial enrichment
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction tests a distinct mechanism of toughness degradation—interstitial embrittlement—in compositionally complex alloys under technical service conditions, thereby providing a clear controlled comparison to the conventional precipitation or segregation phenomena.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. It proposes testing whether interstitial atom segregation at grain boundaries leads to ductility loss in a single-phase HEA, which is a distinct mechanism from those in conventional alloys.
critiques.constraints: It uses the FeCoNiCrMn FCC HEA and remains within the requirement of preserving a compositionally complex alloy. However, the treatment conditions (600°C for 2–4 hours) need careful tuning to retain the single-phase structure.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically plausible; interstitial atoms are known to segregate to GBs and can lower cohesion. In this context, controlled carburizing/nitriding is a reasonable approach.
critiques.feasibility: The intervention can be achieved with established carburizing/nitriding methods and standard mechanical tests (bending and tensile).
critiques.evidence: Records indicate examples of interstitial effects during processing (e.g., PMC10003886, PMC6897545), although prior work focused on avoiding carbide formation. This supports the possibility but also hints at the risk of unintended carbide precipitation.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that the treatment might induce unintended carbide/nitride precipitation rather than merely promoting interstitial segregation, thereby confounding the test of GB embrittlement.
critiques.fix: Refine the temperature and duration of the interstitial doping treatment to ensure that the FCC phase is preserved without triggering carbide/nitride precipitation.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. It directly addresses the open question by testing whether stress-assisted short-range order formation at GBs leads to brittle failure, contrasting with conventional precipitate mechanisms.
critiques.constraints: The approach respects the HEA’s single-phase FCC microstructure and stays within typical processing methods. Service and loading conditions (high strain rate pre-straining and moderate anneal) are also compatible.
critiques.physical_soundness: The hypothesis that mechanical deformation combined with annealing could promote localized SRO at GBs is plausible; however, the effect of such ordering on cohesive strength in HEAs is less well established.
critiques.feasibility: High strain rate pre-straining followed by a controlled anneal are standard practices, and the detection of SRO can be attempted using diffraction and high-resolution TEM.
critiques.evidence: The provided evidence focuses largely on dislocation dynamics and grain boundary behavior (e.g., PMC10131849, PMC12061292), but does not directly address SRO formation. This leaves a gap in direct prior verification.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is the potential difficulty in achieving and reliably detecting the short-range ordering at the grain boundaries, making the link between SRO and toughness degradation ambiguous.
critiques.fix: Integrate complementary characterization techniques (e.g., atom probe tomography or advanced synchrotron diffraction) to unambiguously identify SRO at GBs and correlate it with toughness measurements.

critiques.physical_soundness: The concept that refractory elements can segregate and cause local stiffness mismatches is somewhat plausible, but it is less directly connected to the traditional GB segregation mechanisms in single-phase HEAs. It might inadvertently trigger precipitation.
critiques.feasibility: Alloying with tungsten via arc melting and homogenization is standard; however, controlling its segregation to remain subtle rather than forming detectable phases may be challenging.

critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that tungsten addition may lead to uncontrolled segregation or second-phase precipitation, which would not isolate the testable mechanism of toughness degradation in a single-phase HEA.
critiques.fix: Implement more rigorous phase stability analyses (e.g., via differential scanning calorimetry and high-resolution microstructural characterization) to ensure tungsten remains in solution and induces only subtle heterogeneity, avoiding large precipitate formation.

critiques.constraints: The approach respects the material system (CoCrFeMnNi FCC single-phase) and utilizes a thermal treatment designed to promote subtle segregation without triggering bulk precipitation, keeping within service-relevant boundaries.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is grounded in well-known alloy behavior: even slight GB segregation can reduce cohesive strength and promote crack initiation. This is physically sound and transferable to the HEA context.
critiques.feasibility: Controlled thermal aging is a well-established process, and modern characterization techniques (atom probe tomography, etc.) can verify the segregation. However, care is needed to avoid inadvertent precipitation.
critiques.evidence: This direction is supported by multiple literature records (e.g., PMC6897545, PMC7311485, and PMC4145285) that detail how even subtle GB segregation influences ductility and toughness, especially at low temperatures.

critiques.fix: Fine-tune the aging temperature and duration (using preliminary studies) to ensure that only atomic-scale segregation occurs without transitioning into coarse precipitate formation.

decision.rationale: Option D directly tests whether subtle grain-boundary segregation in a single-phase HEA is responsible for brittleness, a mechanism that contrasts with conventional precipitation‐caused embrittlement. This approach leverages well‐established thermal aging methods and benefits from supporting evidence that GB segregation can weaken cohesion (as seen in PMC6897545, PMC7311485, and PMC4145285). Although there is a risk of inadvertently triggering coarse precipitate formation, this can be managed by fine-tuning the aging temperature and duration. Therefore, we adopt direction D with the recommended adjustments.
